original_question: How quickly do the sequences {ms_r(n)/n}_{n=1}^∞ and {bms_r(n)/n}_{n=1}^∞ converge to their common limit ms_r(I) = bms_r(I)?
target_in_paper: Section 6, Problem 6.6: "How quickly do the sequences {ms_r(n)/n}_{n=1}^∞ and {bms_r(n)/n}_{n=1}^∞ converge to their limit ms_r(I)=bms_r(I)?"
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact official target almost verbatim: it identifies the two normalized sequences from Section 6, asks about their rate of convergence, and correctly uses the common limit ms_r(I)=bms_r(I) supplied by the nearby theorem. It is tightly scoped to the interval problem and does not drift to neighboring questions such as computing ms_r(I) itself or evaluating special cases only.
missing_details: The parameter r should be fixed explicitly; to speak of the common limit ms_r(I)=bms_r(I) in the paper-faithful way, one should impose r>1, because Theorem 6.2(4) gives bms_r(I)=ms_r(I) under that hypothesis.
The symbol n is not just an index: it denotes the finite ordinal n={0,1,...,n-1} viewed as a subset of Z with the counting measure.
The symbol I should be defined as the unit interval I=[0,1] in R.

ms_r(n) should be defined: it is the maximal symmetry number for r-colorings of n, where symmetry is with respect to the family of maps \tilde{s}_c(x)=c-x, c in Z, and size is measured by cardinality.

ms_r(I) should be defined: it is the maximal symmetry number for measurable r-colorings of I, where symmetry is with respect to the central symmetries s_c(x)=2c-x, c in R, and size is measured by Lebesgue measure.
bms_r(n) and bms_r(I) should be defined as blurred maximal symmetry numbers, not ordinary coloring invariants.
A blurred r-coloring should be specified as a family {\chi_i}_{i=1}^r of measurable functions \chi_i:X->[0,1] with sum_i \chi_i equiv 1.
The blurred invariant bms_r(X) is defined through the overlap expression sup_i sup_s integral_X \chi_i(x)\chi_i(s(x)) d\mu_X, which is part of the paper's setup for Section 6.
The convergence is the limit as n->∞.
The phrase "their common limit" is justified by Theorem 6.2(1), (2), and (4); it is not self-contained unless that theorem's conclusion is built into the question.
refined_question: For a fixed integer r>1, let I=[0,1] be endowed with Lebesgue measure and the family of central symmetries s_c(x)=2c-x for c in R, and let n={0,1,...,n-1} subset Z be endowed with the counting measure and the symmetries \tilde{s}_c(x)=c-x for c in Z. Let ms_r(X) denote the maximal symmetry number of X, i.e. the infimum over all measurable r-colorings of X of the largest measure/cardinality of a monochromatic subset A subset X with A=s(A) for some admissible symmetry s, and let bms_r(X) denote the corresponding blurred maximal symmetry number obtained by taking the infimum over measurable blurred r-colorings {\chi_i}_{i=1}^r with \chi_i:X->[0,1] and sum_i \chi_i equiv 1. Since Theorem 6.2 shows that ms_r(I)=lim_{n->∞} ms_r(n)/n, bms_r(I)=lim_{n->∞} bms_r(n)/n, and ms_r(I)=bms_r(I), determine how quickly the normalized sequences ms_r(n)/n and bms_r(n)/n converge, as n->∞, to their common limit ms_r(I)=bms_r(I).
justification: The draft is essentially the paper's official open problem in Section 6. The exact nearest formulation is Problem 6.6, and the surrounding context needed to make it stand-alone comes from the opening paragraphs of Section 6 together with the general definition of ms_r in Section 3 and the definition of blurred r-colorings and bms_r immediately before Theorem 6.2. The phrase "common limit" is justified by Theorem 6.2(1), (2), and (4). So the right refinement is not a broader question, but the same Problem 6.6 with the paper's notation, spaces, symmetry families, measurability assumptions, and the restriction r>1 made explicit.
